context: I. I NTRODUCTION The dynamic shortest path problem is a classic problem in graph algorithms that seeks to maintain the shortest path distances between pairs of vertices in a graph as the graph is subject to updates such as edge insertions, deletions, or weight changes. This problem and its variants have been extensively studied in the theoretical computer science literature, and different algorithmic approaches have been proposed and analyzed depending on the nature of the updates (incremental [2]– [7], decremental [8]–[16] or fully dynamic [17]–[26]) and the type of queries (st [27]–[29], single-source [30]–[37] or allpairs [38]–[47]). Here, “incremental” refers to the setting with only edge insertions, “decremental” to only edge deletions, and “fully dynamic” to the general setting where a graph undergoes both insertions and deletions. Open Problem 1. Can one maintain fully dynamic exact shortest paths in subquadratic time (in the number of vertices n) on unweighted graphs? It was shown by Abboud and Vassilevska Williams [29] that dynamic st-reachability and st-shortest path require algebraic techniques (i.e., fast matrix multiplication) if one hopes to beat the naive O(n2 ) update time algorithm of running BFS/Dijkstra after each update. authors: Jan van den Brand (Georgia Institute of Technology, USA), Adam Karczmarz (University of Warsaw and IDEAS NCBR, Poland)
statement: Open Problem 2. Can fully dynamic st-reachability be solved deterministically in subquadratic time? In other dynamic graph settings, derandomization has received a lot of attention [5], [11], [12], [16], [22], [31], [32], [34], [37], [39], [41], [44], [57], but for fully dynamic reachability with subquadratic update time the question has remained open. In this work, we answer both open problems 1 and 2. We construct a fully dynamic algorithm that maintains exact single-source shortest paths in subquadratic update time, thus providing an answer to open problem 1. This dynamic algorithm is deterministic and works on directed graphs, and can thus solve fully dynamic st-reachability deterministically, solving open problem 2. Finally, the framework that we use is powerful and flexible enough to also yield new worst-case update bounds for fully dynamic (1 + )-approximate all-pairs shortest paths. A. Our results a) SSSP: We present the first fully dynamic algorithm that can maintain exact single source distances, answering open problem 1.

In the previous work, the algebraic perspective requires dynamic algorithms to perform calculations involving very large numbers, and to reduce the bit-length of the numbers involved, past work relied on the randomized SchwartzZippel lemma (i.e., randomized polynomial identity testing) [27], [50], [51] or performing all arithmetic modulo a random prime [52], [53]. As a result, the vast majority of algebraic data structures for dynamic graph problems is randomized [23], [24], [27], [30], [50], [51], [54]–[56]. Deterministic algorithms would be preferable because they allow for greater confidence in their correctness and efficiency, as opposed to randomized algorithms which may only offer probabilistic guarantees on correctness or running time that do not hold in all cases. Moreover, randomized algorithms may restrict the “adversary” creating the sequence of updates from being adaptive. In contrast, deterministic algorithms avoid these issues and allow for more predictable behavior. For algebraic data structures, only in the case of shortest paths in the incremental setting [5] or on undirected graphs in the approximate setting [22] has derandomization been possible, which naturally excludes fully dynamic reachability or fully dynamic shortest paths on directed graphs.
